summary.text: Repeated-squaring computations show that \(28341^{28341}\equiv1\pmod{283411^2}\), while its residues modulo the prime \(283411\) at exponents \(9447,603,423\) are nonunit; since every proper divisor of \(28341=3^2\cdot47\cdot67\) divides one of these three exponents, no proper-divisor cyclotomic factor is divisible by \(283411\). Factoring \(28341^{28341}-1\) as the product of its cyclotomic factors and cancelling the product of the proper-divisor factors, which is coprime to \(283411^2\), puts the full square divisibility into the remaining factor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
n=28341,
\qquad x=28341,
\qquad p=283411,
\qquad N=p^2=80321794921.
\]
We shall prove that
\[
p^2\mid \Phi_n(x).
\]
Taking absolute values will then give the stated divisibility of the sequence value \(a(n)=|\Phi_n(n)|\).

The argument has two parts. First we show that \(p^2\) divides \(x^n-1\). Then, using the cyclotomic factorization of \(x^n-1\), we show that none of the cyclotomic factors indexed by proper divisors of \(n\) is divisible by \(p\). Consequently the entire factor \(p^2\) must occur in \(\Phi_n(x)\).

### 1. The congruence modulo \(p^2\)

We compute \(x^n\) modulo \(N=p^2\) by repeated squaring. For \(j=0,1,\ldots,14\), the residues of \(x^{2^j}\) modulo \(N\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
j&2^j&x^{2^j}\pmod N\\ \hline
0&1&28341\\
1&2&803212281\\
2&4&10305286175\\
3&8&56856623504\\
4&16&11119560660\\
5&32&34823658856\\
6&64&7305860158\\
7&128&72720565854\\
8&256&77339958728\\
9&512&48530202121\\
10&1024&18484540212\\
11&2048&77970117019\\
12&4096&39630026099\\
13&8192&23437256541\\
14&16384&8780247748
\end{array}
\]
Each row after the first is obtained by squaring the residue in the preceding row and reducing modulo \(80321794921\).

The binary decomposition of the exponent is
\[
28341=1+4+16+32+128+512+1024+2048+8192+16384.
\]
Multiplying the corresponding entries of the table, reducing after each multiplication, gives the following accumulation chain:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
e&x^e\pmod N\\ \hline
1&28341\\
5&12069152919\\
21&58902886234\\
53&3524814247\\
181&59346352675\\
693&71235197045\\
1717&8309007975\\
3765&79405617822\\
11957&20736622302\\
28341&1
\end{array}
\]
For example, the transition from exponent \(5\) to exponent \(21\) multiplies by the residue for \(x^{16}\), and every other transition is justified similarly. Thus
\[
x^{28341}\equiv 1\pmod{80321794921}.
\]
Since \(80321794921=283411^2\), this proves
\[
p^2\mid x^n-1. \tag{1}
\]

### 2. Three nondivisibility computations modulo \(p\)

We next identify three exponents for which \(x^d-1\) is not divisible by \(p\). Again using repeated squaring, now modulo \(p=283411\), we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
j&2^j&x^{2^j}\pmod p\\ \hline
0&1&28341\\
1&2&25507\\
2&4&178804\\
3&8&125739\\
4&16&213486\\
5&32&99053\\
6&64&91400\\
7&128&137364\\
8&256&214349\\
9&512&36125\\
10&1024&191381\\
11&2048&66576\\
12&4096&99147\\
13&8192&17074\\
14&16384&174968
\end{array}
\]
As before, each row is the square of the preceding residue modulo \(p\).

For the exponent
\[
9447=1+2+4+32+64+128+1024+8192,
\]
the successive products give
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
e&x^e\pmod p\\ \hline
1&28341\\
3&195837\\
7&159665\\
39&113212\\
103&241190\\
231&77260\\
1255&260779\\
9447&153836.
\end{array}
\]
Hence
\[
x^{9447}\equiv153836\not\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{2}
\]

For
\[
603=1+2+8+16+64+512,
\]
the corresponding accumulation is
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
e&x^e\pmod p\\ \hline
1&28341\\
3&195837\\
11&183808\\
27&197861\\
91&39490\\
603&168687,
\end{array}
\]
so
\[
x^{603}\equiv168687\not\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{3}
\]

Finally,
\[
423=1+2+4+32+128+256,
\]
and the products are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
e&x^e\pmod p\\ \hline
1&28341\\
3&195837\\
7&159665\\
39&113212\\
167&208187\\
423&196258.
\end{array}
\]
Therefore
\[
x^{423}\equiv196258\not\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{4}
\]
Equations (2), (3), and (4) say respectively that
\[
p\nmid x^{9447}-1,
\qquad p\nmid x^{603}-1,
\qquad p\nmid x^{423}-1. \tag{5}
\]

### 3. Divisors of \(28341\)

We have the factorization
\[
28341=9\cdot47\cdot67=3^2\cdot47\cdot67.
\]
The numbers \(47\) and \(67\) are prime: trial division by primes no larger than their square roots suffices (for \(47\), test \(2,3,5\); for \(67\), test \(2,3,5,7\)). Thus every divisor \(k\) of \(28341\) has the form
\[
k=3^\alpha47^\beta67^\gamma,
\quad 0\leq\alpha\leq2,
\quad \beta,\gamma\in\{0,1\}.
\]
If \(k\ne28341\), then at least one of the three exponents is smaller than its maximum. We claim that every such proper divisor divides at least one of
\[
9447=3\cdot47\cdot67,
\qquad
603=9\cdot67,
\qquad
423=9\cdot47. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed:

* If \(\alpha\leq1\), then \(k\mid3\cdot47\cdot67=9447\).
* Suppose \(\alpha=2\). If \(\beta=0\), then \(k\mid9\cdot67=603\).
* Suppose \(\alpha=2\) and \(\beta=1\). If \(\gamma=0\), then \(k\mid9\cdot47=423\).
* The only remaining case is \(\alpha=2\), \(\beta=1\), \(\gamma=1\), which gives \(k=28341\) and is excluded.

Thus (6) covers every proper divisor of \(n\).

Now recall the elementary divisibility
\[
u^r-v^r\mid u^{rm}-v^{rm}
\]
for positive integers \(r,m\); this follows from the geometric-series factorization. In particular, if \(k\mid d\), then
\[
x^k-1\mid x^d-1. \tag{7}
\]
Combining (5), (6), and (7), we conclude that for every proper divisor \(k\) of \(n\),
\[
p\nmid x^k-1. \tag{8}
\]
For if \(p\mid x^k-1\), and \(k\) divides one of \(9447,603,423\), then (7) would imply that \(p\) divides the corresponding number in (5), a contradiction.

### 4. Primality of \(283411\)

We will use that \(p=283411\) is prime. Here is a concise arithmetic certificate.

First,
\[
p-1=283410=2\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot47\cdot67,
\]
and all primes in this factorization have already been identified as prime (with \(2,3,5\) immediate and \(47,67\) checked above). Repeated squaring modulo \(p\) gives
\[
2^{283410}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and, for the distinct prime divisors \(q\) of \(p-1\),
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
q&(p-1)/q&2^{(p-1)/q}\pmod p\\ \hline
2&141705&283410\\
3&94470&153836\\
5&56682&174613\\
47&6030&147198\\
67&4230&236184.
\end{array}
\]
None of the residues in the last column is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(p\). More strongly, their differences from \(1\) are coprime to \(p\), as witnessed by the following Bézout identities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
141705\cdot283409-141704\cdot283411&=1,\\
43191\cdot153835-23444\cdot283411&=1,\\
80838\cdot174612-49805\cdot283411&=1,\\
79994\cdot147197-41547\cdot283411&=1,\\
19773\cdot236183-16478\cdot283411&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
These congruences prove primality by the standard order criterion, which we briefly justify. Since \(p\) is odd, \(2\) is a unit modulo \(p\). Its multiplicative order divides \(p-1\), because \(2^{p-1}\equiv1\). If that order were a proper divisor of \(p-1\), then, because the complete prime factorization of \(p-1\) is known, it would divide \((p-1)/q\) for at least one prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\). This would give \(2^{(p-1)/q}\equiv1\pmod p\), contrary to the table. Thus the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is exactly \(p-1\). The order of a unit divides the number of units modulo \(p\), which is at most \(p-1\), and is strictly less than \(p-1\) if \(p\) is composite. Hence \(p\) must be prime.

### 5. Isolating the top cyclotomic factor

For every positive integer \(m\), the cyclotomic polynomials satisfy
\[
X^m-1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(X).
\]
Evaluating at the integer \(x=28341\) gives
\[
x^m-1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(x). \tag{9}
\]
In particular, for any positive divisor \(k\) of \(n\), applying (9) with \(m=k\) shows that
\[
\Phi_k(x)\mid x^k-1. \tag{10}
\]
Combining (8) and (10), we find that for every proper divisor \(k\) of \(n\),
\[
p\nmid\Phi_k(x). \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid\Phi_k(x)\), then (10) would imply \(p\mid x^k-1\), contradicting (8).

Define the product of all the proper-divisor factors by
\[
B=\prod_{\substack{k\mid n\\k\ne n}}\Phi_k(x).
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, if it divided this finite product, it would divide one of its factors. This is impossible by (11). Therefore
\[
p\nmid B,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \gcd(p,B)=1.
\]
It follows also that
\[
\gcd(p^2,B)=1, \tag{12}
\]
since the only prime divisor of \(p^2\) is \(p\).

Taking \(m=n\) in (9) and separating the factor indexed by \(n\), we obtain
\[
x^n-1=\Phi_n(x)B. \tag{13}
\]
By (1), \(p^2\) divides the left side of (13), and hence
\[
p^2\mid \Phi_n(x)B.
\]
But \(p^2\) is coprime to \(B\) by (12). Euclid's lemma therefore gives
\[
p^2\mid\Phi_n(x).
\]
Finally, integer divisibility is preserved upon taking absolute values. Since
\[
a(28341)=\left|\Phi_{28341}(28341)\right|,
\]
we conclude that
\[
283411^2\mid a(28341),
\]
as required.
